title: Wine Wimsey Review · Tue Nov 3
subtitle: 16 feed posts (14 images + 2 TOBIs at #5 and #12) and 4 stories. TOBIs: week 45 is odd, so Tuesday gets 2. Inbox was empty (0 new items) and nothing was held, so every post is new. All character posts are The Hot Mess; #10 is a people-free still life with the AI label. Flags: the WineWimsey stamp sits tight against the last line of text on #3 and story 2 (still readable); captions are about 80-90 words on the long ones.

posts.quote: Nobody warns you that the stairs will start charging a toll of one groan per step.
posts.caption: The staircase in my house has fourteen steps. I've counted, mostly because my knees insist on a running tally. Going down is free. Going up is billed monthly.
posts.first: I carried a laundry basket up Saturday and stopped on step nine to reconsider my life choices. The basket was fine. The cat passed me on the left like I was construction. I finished the climb out of professional courtesy. The rest of the laundry is still down there, making its own plans.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun climbing a carpeted staircase hugging a laundry basket with a pained, amused face. Text in the speech bubble reads: Nobody warns you that the stairs will start charging a toll of one groan per step.

posts.quote: My mother said I'd thank her for the sensible shoes someday. It's Tuesday and I'm thanking her out loud in the shoe aisle.
posts.caption: The shoes are beige. I want that on the record before anything else. They have arch support, a rubber sole, and no opinion about my outfit, which is what I now look for in everything. At twenty-six I would have walked past them like a stranger on a train. Today I held them with both hands and nodded at the box. The salesman asked if I wanted to try them on and I said I'd already decided in my heart. My feet agreed first.
posts.first: She bought me a pair just like these when I was fifteen and I left them in a locker on purpose. I'm not proud of it. I did call her from the parking lot afterward, mostly to say the receipt was in the bag. She laughed for a full minute and said nothing else.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a shoe store holding up a beige comfort shoe with a grateful smile. Text at the top reads: My mother said I'd thank her for the sensible shoes someday. It's Tuesday and I'm thanking her out loud in the shoe aisle.

posts.quote: I put on one calm documentary about a missing lighthouse keeper and the news didn't find me for three whole hours.
posts.caption: Narrator with a soft voice, a blanket, and a mystery from 1962 that has no push notifications. I'd like to thank everyone involved. The keeper is still missing and I've never felt more rested.
posts.first: The documentary was three episodes. I watched all three and then started a fourth about a different lighthouse. Nobody was lost in that one, which felt like a letdown. I fell asleep around eleven with the remote on my chest and the sea doing its thing in the background.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun curled under a blanket on a couch beside a sleeping dog and cat with a glass of red wine, watching a TV showing a lighthouse in a storm. Text at the top reads: I put on one calm documentary about a missing lighthouse keeper. Text at the bottom reads: and the news didn't find me for three whole hours.

posts.quote: I caught my reflection in the microwave door and said sorry before I realized it was me.
posts.caption: The microwave door is black glass and tells no lies. I was reaching for the leftover soup when a woman with a bun and a pencil in it stepped into my space. I said sorry. She said nothing, which I took as forgiveness. It took two full seconds for the pieces to connect, and the soup was already beeping. The pencil, for the record, has been in my hair since lunch. I've noticed it now and chosen to leave it.
posts.first: Last month I waved at a woman through the bakery window and she waved back with the same exact hand. It was a mirror. I bought a muffin anyway so the afternoon wouldn't be a total loss. The muffin was stale. It still outranked the wave.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a bowl of soup in a kitchen, apologizing to her faint reflection in a microwave door. Text in the speech bubble reads: I caught my reflection in the microwave door and said sorry before I realized it was me.

posts.quote: Somewhere between thirty and now, I became a person who checks the weather before deciding how to feel about the day.
posts.first: I checked the forecast three times before breakfast and then stood at the window to confirm it. Rain, apparently, was the plan. I put the umbrella by the door like a person with a system. The sky has not commented, but I felt a certain closeness with it.

posts.quote: My financial advisor said to think long term. I thought about Thursday and had to lie down.
posts.caption: He had charts. Colored ones, with arrows. I nodded at the arrows and wrote down 'index' because it looked official. The meeting lasted forty minutes and I came out with a pen and a mild headache.
posts.first: I got home and put the folder on the counter next to the toaster, where it will wait with the others. The pen, at least, writes well. I've been using it to make lists of things I plan to look into. There are four so far.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a hand to her forehead with a wine glass in the other hand and a chart folder under her arm. Text beside her reads: My financial advisor said to think long term. I thought about Thursday and had to lie down.

posts.quote: The pharmacy gave me a bag for one tiny bottle and a receipt as long as my arm. I felt very well looked after.
posts.caption: I waited eleven minutes for a bottle the size of my thumb. The woman behind the counter put it in a bag, stapled the top shut, and added a receipt that kept coming like a magic trick. Then she asked me to confirm my birthday out loud, in front of everyone. I said it clearly. Nobody in the line looked up. It's strange how comforting a stapled bag can be. I carried it out with both hands like a diploma.
posts.first: At home the bottle sat on the counter next to its own receipt, which was longer than the grocery receipt from Saturday. I measured. It made it to the fridge door under a magnet shaped like a lemon. If anyone needs the information on that receipt, it's well displayed.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a pharmacy counter holding a small stapled paper bag and a very long receipt, looking proud. Text in the speech bubble reads: The pharmacy gave me a bag for one tiny bottle and a receipt as long as my arm. I felt very well looked after.

posts.quote: The self-checkout said 'unexpected item in the bagging area.' It was my purse. I've been called worse by better machines.
posts.caption: I'd scanned eleven items without a hint of trouble. Then the machine turned on me over a handbag I've owned since 2014. An attendant came over, tapped the screen twice, and everything was fine again. Nobody apologized. I held my purse a little tighter.
posts.first: The attendant's name tag said Dale. He has seen things. He looked at me the way a lifeguard looks at a swimmer who's fine but insists on waving. I thanked him and he said 'happens all the time.' I chose to believe that for the whole drive home.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a self-checkout with her handbag on the scale, arms crossed, glaring at the screen. Text at the top reads: The self-checkout said 'unexpected item in the bagging area.' It was my purse. I've been called worse by better machines.

posts.quote: My friend says she wakes up at five feeling refreshed. I've decided to stay friends anyway.
posts.caption: She told me this at lunch, cheerfully, as if she were reading a menu. Five o'clock. Refreshed. She said the word 'stretch' twice. I stirred my soup and tried to look like a person who understood any of it. At five o'clock, my body is still negotiating the terms of the night before and has not yet been introduced to my brain. We have an arrangement, the two of us, and it involves a pillow over my head until at least seven. She's lovely. I keep her around for the stories.
posts.first: My alarm went off at six thirty today and I said good morning to it like an old coworker. Then I hit snooze twice, out of respect for tradition. By seven I was upright, which counts. My friend sent a photo of her sunrise walk around then. The sun looked fine without me.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun stirring a bowl of soup at a cafe table with a deadpan sideways glance. Text in the speech bubble reads: My friend says she wakes up at five feeling refreshed. I've decided to stay friends anyway.

posts.quote: The song from my first car came on in the dentist's waiting room and I knew every word. Nobody there knew me, and they know me now.
posts.caption: I tried to hold it together at first. By the second chorus my foot had joined in. The woman with the magazine looked up once, then went back to her page with great dignity. The hygienist called my name in the middle of the bridge, which felt personal.
posts.first: That cassette lived in a 1991 sedan with a window that only went halfway down. I played it until the tape stretched and the singer started sounding underwater. I still think she sounded better that way. The dentist said my teeth were fine. I said it was the song.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun singing loudly in a dentist's waiting room while two other patients peek over magazines. Text at the top reads: The song from my first car came on in the dentist's waiting room and I knew every word. Nobody there knew me, and they know me now.

posts.quote: Tuesday asked nothing of me, so I gave it nothing back, and we parted on good terms.
posts.caption: A blanket, a book I've held for six days, and the porch light doing most of the work. The evening went by without a single reminder, notification, or sound from the dryer. I'll take it.
posts.first: The book's still on page forty-one. I've read that page maybe five times and it's very good. Somewhere around eight the porch light flickered on, then off, then on again. It seemed to be thinking about it, same as me. We both stayed put.
posts.alt: Still life photo of a quiet autumn porch at dusk with a knit blanket, a closed book, a glass of red wine and a small lantern on a wooden table. Text at the top reads: Tuesday asked nothing of me, so I gave it nothing back, and we parted on good terms.

posts.quote: I turned to look at the doorbell camera and my neck filed a formal complaint.
posts.caption: The camera sent me a notification at 2:14 in the afternoon: 'Person detected.' It was the mail carrier, dropping off a flyer for a gutter company. I rushed to the window, turned my head too fast, and heard something go click in a place I didn't know had parts. My neck has since taken a firm position. I'm currently holding my head at an angle that suggests I'm listening very carefully to someone on my left. The flyer is quite persuasive about gutters.
posts.first: The heating pad has been on my neck for an hour and I've worked out which pillow works best. It's the flat one, the one I never use, which tells you everything about how this week is going. The doorbell chimed again around four. A squirrel. I let him handle it.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in an entryway wincing with her head twisted and a hand on her neck, holding a phone. Text in the speech bubble reads: I turned to look at the doorbell camera and my neck filed a formal complaint.

posts.quote: I keep seven dead pens by the phone for the day one of them changes its mind.
posts.first: The cup by the phone holds seven pens and a pair of scissors that cut nothing. Last week one of the pens wrote a full grocery list, then stopped forever. I've decided it was giving a farewell address. The other six are paying close attention.

posts.quote: The cable company offered me a new customer deal. I've been a customer for nineteen years. I felt like a ghost at my own funeral.
posts.caption: The woman on the phone was lovely and reading from a script. I'm told the deal is for people who haven't been here. I'd like to point out that I have, in fact, been here since the flip phone. She put me on hold to check. I stared at the junk drawer instead.
posts.first: In the end they knocked six dollars off for 'loyalty,' which they described like it was a trophy. I said thank you and meant maybe half of it. The remote's batteries died during the call. I decided it was a sign and went to find some.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a sofa with a phone at her ear and a wine glass in hand, looking unimpressed, with cable bills on the table. Text at the top reads: The cable company offered me a new customer deal. I've been a customer for nineteen years. I felt like a ghost at my own funeral.

posts.quote: My doctor said my numbers look great for my age. I asked which age, and she changed the subject.
posts.caption: She had the chart open on a laptop and kept scrolling past things she didn't mention. I watched her eyes, like you watch a waiter carrying someone else's order. Cholesterol, fine. Blood pressure, fine. 'For your age' appeared twice, each time with a small pause in front. I thanked her for the good news. She printed me a page of instructions I won't read until the weekend. I carried it out feeling oddly proud, like a student who passed without studying.
posts.first: The page of instructions is on the fridge beside the gutter flyer. It looks like a small museum of me being looked after. I read the first line on Sunday. It said 'Drink more water.' I'm working my way up to the second line.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting on an exam table squinting at a doctor in a white coat who is looking at a laptop. Text in the speech bubble reads: My doctor said my numbers look great for my age. I asked which age, and she changed the subject.

posts.quote: I was told there'd be wisdom. So far I've got a drawer of dead batteries and strong opinions about parking lots.
posts.caption: At forty I assumed wisdom would arrive like a package, signature required. By fifty I'd stopped checking the porch. What showed up instead was a gradual, unglamorous collection: the batteries, the rubber bands, the certainty that the person who parks diagonally across two spaces is doing it on purpose. I've also acquired a firm view on the correct way to load a dishwasher. If that's wisdom, it's less shiny than advertised. It's mine, though, and it's well organized, and the batteries are labeled.
posts.first: I tested the batteries on Sunday with the kitchen timer and a flashlight, which was a full afternoon's work. Four turned out to be good. I put them back in the drawer, next to the ones that aren't, so everyone could feel included. Nobody can tell them apart, and that's the real wisdom.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a drawer full of batteries and a glass of red wine with a wry smirk. Text beside her reads: I was told there'd be wisdom. So far I've got a drawer of dead batteries and strong opinions about parking lots.

stories.quote: Sweater weather brought the static back. I shocked the cat, the cat shocked me, and we both took it personally.
stories.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a chunky sweater touching a startled cat with static-raised fur, small sparks between them. Text at the top reads: Sweater weather brought the static back. I shocked the cat, the cat shocked me, and we both took it personally.

stories.quote: The leaves are down and the porch is buried. The rake and I have agreed to some space.
stories.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting on a leaf-covered porch step holding a mug, a rake leaning far behind her. Text at the top reads: The leaves are down and the porch is buried. Text at the bottom reads: The rake and I have agreed to some space.

stories.quote: Made a pot of soup big enough for a church. Eating it until Friday. No regrets, only containers.
stories.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a ladle and a stack of containers beside a huge pot of soup, grinning. Text beside her reads: Made a pot of soup big enough for a church. Eating it until Friday. No regrets, only containers.

stories.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sprawled on a sofa under a blanket holding a remote and a glass of red wine, a cat asleep beside her, smiling serenely.
